references.text: Daniel asks, "How long will it be before these wonderful things come to an end?" – the same type of question about end-time signs and timing, as the disciples ask Jesus in [ref:Luk 21:7|Luke 21:7].

The parallel passage in [ref:Matt 24:3|Matthew 24:3] where the disciples ask Jesus on the Mount of Olives: "When will this happen, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?" – the same question about timing and signs.

The parallel passage in [ref:Mark 13:4|Mark 13:4] where the disciples ask: "When will this happen, and what will be the sign that all these things are about to be fulfilled?" – an identical question to Luke's version.

After the resurrection, the disciples ask Jesus: "Lord, is this the time when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?" ([ref:Apg 1:6-7|Acts 1:6-7]). Jesus again rejects that they should know times and seasons – the same theme of asking about the timing of God's plan.

In [ref:Luk 19:43-44|Luke 19:43-44], Jesus prophesies about Jerusalem's destruction, where enemies will level the city to the ground and not leave one stone upon another – the prophecy that forms the background for the disciples' question in 21:7.

The immediate context in [ref:Luk 21:5-6|Luke 21:5-6], where Jesus predicts that not one stone will be left upon another in the temple, which prompts the disciples to ask when this will happen and what the sign will be.
Jesus answers the question from verse 7 by giving the sign: "When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its destruction is near" ([ref:Luk 21:20-22|Luke 21:20-22]).

Paul writes about "times and seasons" and warns against false security ([ref:1 Tess 5:1-3|1 Thessalonians 5:1-3]) – thematically linked to the question of when end-time events will occur and what signs will precede them.
